name: Investments tied to one partner
idea: Specific assets can be moved to other uses or users only at a loss of value, so continuity matters. In some deals, many qualified suppliers at the outset become, in effect, a two-party relation once the contract runs. Left unprotected, such investments pose a hazard that far-sighted parties price in. One firm owning both sides comes in only as specificity and uncertainty rise.
suggests: Look at what a company has built for one customer, supplier or site, ask what it would be worth anywhere else, and check what protects it if that relationship turns sour.
limits: The work finds contracting under fully stable conditions uninteresting; on its account, the choice between market and firm becomes engaging only once unplanned adaptations are needed.
competing_idea: Another view holds that dissimilar activities which must be co-ordinated generally fall to different firms, which then match their plans in advance by co-operating or rely on market adjustment.
questions: What would this asset be worth if the customer, supplier or site it was built for went away?
Once the investment is made, how many other partners could the company realistically turn to?
What protects the investment if the partner turns difficult: a long contract, penalties, shared ownership, or nothing?

originals.reference: Oliver E. Williamson, "The Economics of Governance" (Richard T. Ely Lecture), AEA Papers and Proceedings, Vol. 95 No. 2, May 2005, pp. 1-18
G. B. Richardson, "The Organisation of Industry", The Economic Journal, Vol. 82 No. 327, Sept. 1972, pp. 883-896
